Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a common type of skin cancer that arises from basal cells in the epidermis. It is characterized by abnormal growth of these cells, often caused by DNA damage from ultraviolet radiation.

Organ transplant recipients are individuals who have received an organ transplant and take immunosuppressive medicines to prevent graft rejection. This immunosuppression increases their risk of developing basal cell carcinoma.
Ultraviolet radiation is a form of electromagnetic radiation from the sun or artificial sources. It can damage DNA in skin cells and is a major risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma.
Skin cells are the cells in the epidermis that can be damaged by ultraviolet radiation, and their DNA damage is a precursor to basal cell carcinoma development.

Immunosuppressive medicines are drugs that reduce the activity of the immune system. They are used in organ transplant recipients to prevent graft rejection but weaken immune surveillance, increasing the risk of skin cancers like BCC.
